title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 10: Offering to the Father
keywords: Father into your hands I commend my spirit
primary_topics: Chapter 10 of 'Justice and Faith' -- CJP's Holy Friday reflection on Jesus's last words from the cross, Luke 23:46 ('Father, into your hands, I commend my spirit'), framed as the universal call to commend our daily work and decisions to the Father in imitation of Christ

A pluralist account of how Christians imitate Christ -- hermits and contemplatives, priests and missionaries, numeraries and nuns, even flagellants, but most centrally ordinary lay people in workplaces, boardrooms, schools and streets -- Mother Teresa's 'We are all called to be Christ to others'

An autobiographical confession of restlessness -- CJP's many years of working and wheeling produced power, position, possession, yet 'no peace and quiet; no fulfillment or sense of purpose' until he committed himself to the Father and recognized himself as 'a citizen of heaven' even while a resident of earth
A closing pledge in oath form -- 'I hold my present office, my life and my time by God's grace...I commend to Him all my work, actions and decisions'
sub_topics: Opening -- Christ's last words (Lk 23:46) as the perfect obedience of the Son to the Father, His death freely and happily chosen

Vignette of grandson Miggy -- six years old at Southridge School preschool, outstanding-pupil award, told CJP he 'studied hard, did not watch television except during holidays, woke up early, did my homework every day,' then placed the certificate at the home altar -- sacrifice and offering as a single act in a child's hands
Christian imitations of Christ catalogue -- contemplative hermits, men and women of the cloth, missionaries, devoted flagellants -- read as a pluralist taxonomy of vocations
Mother Teresa quotation -- 'We are all called to be Christ to others so that others may become Christ to still many others'

Ordinary vocations as Christ-bearing -- student studying hard offers his grades; policeman patrolling his beat with honesty fosters peace; housewife preparing meals serves the Lord; husband working honestly commends his life to Jesus; businessman selling quality at reasonable prices pleases the Father; government functionary discharging duties with integrity lifts up his work as Christ on the cross
St. Augustine -- 'our hearts are restless until they rest in God'

The walking-wounded image -- 'all of us have suffered illness, pain, spiritual emptiness, psychological affliction and social deprivation...pretending to be whole and healthy, but in truth longing for healing, love and peace'

CJP's personal testimony -- 'many years ago I was a restless young man in search of fame and fortune'; many years of working and wheeling produced power, possession and convenience but no peace, no fulfillment; the questions 'Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for?'

Conversion narrative -- committing to the Father, acknowledging the Holy Spirit's loving presence, proclaiming Jesus as 'Lord and Savior, Healer and Friend,' learning the purpose is to obey and glorify God
The 'resident of earth, citizen of heaven' formula as the orienting self-identity

Closing dedicatory pledge -- 'all my actions and decisions will only be in accordance with His commandments and His gospel. I hold my present office...by God's grace...I commend to Him all my work, actions and decisions'
Closing prayer -- 'O, Heavenly Father, into Your hands we commend our work, our minds, our lives and our spirits. Amen'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 10 of 'Justice and Faith' is CJP's Holy Friday reflection on Luke 23:46 ('Father, into your hands, I commend my spirit'), the last words of Jesus on the cross, framed as a paradigm of perfect obedience that every disciple is invited to imitate in daily work and decisions. He opens with a vignette of his six-year-old grandson Miggy, who told him he earned a preschool outstanding-pupil award at Southridge School by studying hard, watching no TV except during holidays, waking early, and doing his homework every day -- then placed the certificate at the home altar, a child's complete sacrifice-and-offering. CJP then catalogues the plural Christian imitations of Christ -- contemplative hermits, priests and nuns, missionaries who 'sail the seven seas,' even flagellants -- before turning to the most ordinary form, citing Mother Teresa: 'We are all called to be Christ to others so that others may become Christ to still many others.' He develops this with a litany of ordinary vocations: a student offering his grades, a policeman patrolling honestly, a housewife preparing meals lovingly, a husband working faithfully, a businessman selling quality at reasonable prices, a government functionary discharging duties in integrity -- each lifts work to the Lord as Christ did on the cross. Augustine's 'our hearts are restless until they rest in God' anchors a walking-wounded image of humanity; CJP supplies his own confession -- a restless young man chasing fame, fortune, power, position and possession that produced no peace and no fulfillment ('Who am I? Why was I born? Where am I headed for?'). Only when he committed to the Father, acknowledged the Holy Spirit, and proclaimed Jesus as 'Lord and Savior, Healer and Friend' did the dual-citizenship orientation arrive: a resident of earth, truly a citizen of heaven. He closes with a dedicatory pledge in oath form -- 'I hold my present office -- as indeed my life and my time -- by God's grace' -- and a closing prayer: 'O, Heavenly Father, into Your hands we commend our work, our minds, our lives and our spirits. Amen.'
